title: The Smiling Visitor
premise: Kestrel Quintana returns to the family homestead to bury their twin, Wren — except the body in the casket wears Kestrel's face, and everyone in town insists Kestrel is the one who died. Haunted by sleep recordings in which a second voice answers questions Kestrel never asked aloud, they uncover the old well on the property: a mouth that refills every generation, fed by a lullaby whose final verse was cut from the family songbook. The voice in the recordings is Wren, not dead but traded, kept singing below to hold the water down. To free them, Kestrel must learn the last verse from the thing wearing their mother's smile — without ever singing along — and seal the well before it refills, at the cost of surrendering every memory of the sibling they came home to save.
about_author: Emrys Lockridge is the pen name of a former hospice night nurse from coastal Maine who spent years listening to what patients said in their sleep. Their fiction explores grief as an architecture, and they claim never to write after midnight — a rule they broke exactly once.

chapters.title: The Wrong Body
chapters.summary: Kestrel arrives for the funeral and finds the casket open: the corpse has their own face. The funeral director calls them by Wren's name; their mother greets them like a stranger. POV: Kestrel. Emotional beat: disorientation curdling into dread — the first sign that coming home was itself the trap.

chapters.title: Doors Counted Twice
chapters.summary: Kestrel moves into the homestead, keeping ritual habits: lights on, doors counted each night. The count keeps coming out one door too many. A neighbor, Odile Voss, warns them off the back field where the old well sits capped with iron. POV: Kestrel. Emotional beat: fragile control eroding at the edges.

chapters.title: What the Recorder Heard
chapters.summary: Reviewing their sleep-app recordings to check for night terrors, Kestrel hears a second voice — soft, familiar — answering questions no one asked. The voice says their childhood nickname. They play it forty times until dawn. POV: Kestrel. Emotional beat: terror braided with unbearable hope that it's Wren.

chapters.title: A Town That Mourns You
chapters.summary: Kestrel visits the church archive and finds their own obituary, dated three weeks ago. Townspeople offer condolences to them, gently, as if humoring a ghost. Only Odile treats them as living. POV: Kestrel. Emotional beat: isolation deepening; the world itself seems complicit.

chapters.title: Mother's Smile
chapters.summary: Kestrel's mother, Marisol, invites them to dinner and smiles too long, too evenly, telling stories of Wren that contradict everything Kestrel remembers. Her teeth are wrong in the lamplight. POV: Kestrel. Emotional beat: the horror of doubting your own memories against a parent's warmth.

chapters.title: The Capped Well
chapters.summary: Defying Odile, Kestrel walks the back field at dusk. The iron cap over the well is warm, humming faintly, and frost circles it in summer heat. Scratched inside the rust: half a verse of the family lullaby. POV: Kestrel. Emotional beat: awe tipping into obsession.

chapters.title: Questions Answered
chapters.summary: Kestrel begins asking questions aloud before sleeping so the recorder will catch the second voice's replies. The voice knows things only Wren knew — and warns, once: 'Stop asking. It learns the shape of wanting.' POV: Kestrel, with recorded interludes. Emotional beat: intimacy with something that may be baiting them.

chapters.title: Odile's Ledger
chapters.summary: Odile reveals she is the last of a line of 'well-keepers,' showing a ledger of Quintana trades across generations: a name given, a name taken, the song sung to settle accounts. Every entry ends mid-verse. POV: alternating Kestrel and Odile. Emotional beat: the relief of explanation shadowed by its implications.

chapters.title: Wren Below
chapters.summary: Through the recorder, Kestrel coaxes the truth: Wren traded themselves years ago to save Marisol, and has been singing below ever since to keep the water down. The song is failing. Wren's voice grows hoarse across nights. POV: Kestrel. Emotional beat: guilt igniting — survival already purchased with a sibling.

chapters.title: The Cut Verse
chapters.summary: In the attic, Kestrel finds the family songbook with the lullaby's final page razored out. Beneath the floorboard where it lay: a child's drawing of two stick figures, one holding the other above dark water. POV: Kestrel. Emotional beat: tenderness and violation entwined — someone erased the way out.

chapters.title: Marisol Remembers Wrong
chapters.summary: Confronted, Marisol recites the lullaby flawlessly — then keeps going past where it should end, eyes glazed, smiling. Kestrel flees as her voice doubles beneath itself. She isn't possessed; she's rehearsed. POV: Kestrel. Emotional beat: betrayal — the mother is the well's choir director.

chapters.title: Refilling
chapters.summary: The well begins to refill early: wells in town run black, birds circle the field in slow spirals, and the recorder captures dozens of voices now, all humming. Odile's ledger pages blank themselves. POV: Odile. Emotional beat: the stakes widen from one family to the whole valley.

chapters.title: The Price of Survival
chapters.summary: Odile explains the rule plainly: the last verse can be learned only by hearing it whole, but anyone who sings even a syllable of it belongs to the well. Knowledge itself is the trap. Kestrel must memorize without voicing. POV: Odile. Emotional beat: cold clarity — the theme made mechanical.

chapters.title: Night Choir
chapters.summary: Kestrel sleeps wired to recorders and dreams in harmony, waking with the melody lodged behind their teeth, lips moving unbidden. They bind their own mouth with cloth at night. The second voice begs them to stop coming closer. POV: Kestrel. Emotional beat: self-becoming-battleground.

chapters.title: What Marisol Traded
chapters.summary: Digging through Marisol's locked trunk, Kestrel learns the original trade: decades ago, Marisol gave one twin's future to the well to survive a fever — choosing which child would owe. Wren volunteered to pay it early. POV: flashback chapters framed by Kestrel reading letters. Emotional beat: rage and grief fused.

chapters.title: The Smiling Visitor
chapters.summary: The thing wearing Marisol's smile visits Kestrel directly, offering the last verse freely if Kestrel will simply sing it back as confirmation. It speaks in Wren's cadence. Kestrel refuses, and the visitor's smile splits wider than a face allows. POV: Kestrel. Emotional beat: temptation at maximum; power offered as corruption.

chapters.title: Silent Lessons
chapters.summary: Kestrel devises a method: the visitor sings, Kestrel transcribes notation by hand, learning pitch and word visually, never aloud. Nights of silent study while the house hums and the water rises audibly beneath the floorboards. POV: Kestrel. Emotional beat: grim discipline — love expressed as restraint.

chapters.title: Odile Breaks
chapters.summary: The well takes Odile's granddaughter as collateral pressure. Odile, desperate, tries to sing the verse herself to force a trade and is pulled to the cap, mouth filling with cold water though she stands dry land. Kestrel saves her by humming — silently, in their head — breaking the melody's pull. POV: Odile. Emotional beat: ally nearly lost; the enemy adapts.

chapters.title: The Refill
chapters.summary: On the solstice the well uncaps itself. Black water climbs the field, and every sleeper in town sits up at midnight, mouths open, waiting for a lead voice. Marisol walks toward the well singing. Kestrel has one night left. POV: multiple, converging. Emotional beat: apocalyptic pressure; no more time to be careful.

chapters.title: The Last Verse
chapters.summary: At the well's edge, Kestrel faces the visitor and Wren's exhausted voice below. They speak-sing the final verse — words pitched, not voiced, a loophole carved from silence — commanding the water to account for itself. The well demands a singer. Kestrel offers the one thing permitted: their memories of Wren, every one. POV: Kestrel. Emotional beat: climax — sacrifice reframed as payment, not loss of life but loss of remembrance.

chapters.title: Aftertaste of Water
chapters.summary: The well seals. Wren emerges alive but a stranger to Kestrel, who remembers having a twin the way you remember a dream — warm, formless. Wren grieves being known and unknown at once, and chooses to stay anyway, teaching Kestrel who they were. POV: alternating twins. Emotional beat: bittersweet resolution; survival's price paid in identity.

chapters.title: One Door Too Many
chapters.summary: Months later, the homestead is quiet, the doors count true, and the recorder gathers dust. But one night it switches on alone and captures two voices laughing — and a third, far off, patiently humming the first line of a new song. Kestrel unplugs it and counts the doors twice. POV: Kestrel. Emotional beat: earned peace with a hairline crack — memory fades, but vigilance endures.
